summary:
We built a 2D mission-control game for kids, where you sent 5 astronauts to the moon and now they can't get home. You are running Mission Control: read their help calls, plan rescues, and spend power, air and radiation shielding wisely. Sun storms built from real solar flare data (NASA DONKI, with a labelled NOAA backup) force hard choices. You have to keep everyone healthy and bring them all home.

This teaches the player to balance hard choices like planning their resources ahead of time and decision making on the spot.
details:
Lunar Mission Control is a browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. You play Mission Control for 5 astronauts stranded on the Moon. They send help calls for air, power, a tow, a nasi lemak delivery or a ride home. You plan each rescue by choosing a helper, a vehicle (rover or drone) and a route (short or safe).

Three resources compete, so no choice is free. Power makes air tanks and charges the radiation shield, and every rescue trip costs power. When a sun storm warning arrives, you choose to shelter everyone, shelter only the waiting crew, or keep working. Sheltering protects health but costs shield and pauses rescues. Radiation lowers each astronaut's health. At 0% an astronaut gets sick and must be home within 2.5 hours, or you lose.

Real NASA data drives the storms. Each storm is built from a real M or X class solar flare from NASA DONKI. A bigger real flare makes a longer, costlier storm. If DONKI is unreachable, the game uses NOAA GOES flare data. If both fail, it uses NASA-documented archive storms. The game labels every source as live, archive or saved copy. Science cards use a saved RadLab ISS dose-rate reading, saved OSDR mouse studies, and Canadian Space Agency food facts.

Impact: kids learn that shielding, power and air compete, that bigger flares mean bigger storms, and that radiation adds up over time.

Tools: TypeScript, Vite, plain HTML/CSS, WebAudio, vite-plugin-singlefile. There is no backend or account, and the game builds to one HTML file.

Creative choices: the game is built around pictures instead of reading. Nasi lemak deliveries add a Malaysian touch. Trail surprises and storm timing change every game.

Factors considered:

Only 3 core resources, so young players aren't overwhelmed.
No free choices.
Gentle failure messages.
Honest data labelling.
